title: It’s a Decoy
dateline: Terrinia. The night the base fell.
mood: Lesley rides home to find the city’s edge on fire. From a rooftop she sees where the giant is walking.

hero.alt: Lesley stands alone on a high rooftop ledge at night, her long hair blowing, looking down on a city of towers burning orange below while small craft fly through the smoke.

segs.t: This was the night Lesley’s dream kept. It always ended on a child’s voice.
She rode back toward Terrinia in the back of a Shield truck, among the crates, with her rifle upright between her knees.
The mission was over. She would never tell anyone what it had been.
Nine days.
One more week,
Chang’e had said at the gate. So the first light had come without her, or it was coming tonight.
There would be a fourth plate on the table, set every night, by the chair that faced the door. She had promised to be back. She was nearly back.
The comm at her collar was still dark. Her orders held until she was inside the city.
“Home by one,” the driver called back through the cab window.
Past midnight the truck came over the last hill, and he braked hard.
“That’s the edge,” he said.
The city’s edge was burning.
Sirens ran along it from end to end. Under them came a roar she knew from the station wall.
Lesley was over the tailboard before the truck stopped. She switched the comm on, and the small green light came back.
It had two channels, the base’s and the Shield’s. The dial was still on the base’s, where she had left it.
“Base, this is Lesley. Come in.”
Only hiss.
The base lay far behind this edge, down by the water. Its radio had never reached this far out.
If it’s tonight, they’re at the frame now,
she thought.
Counting.
For a breath she saw it: Chang’e’s palm on the copper plate, the count going up, the light holding in its cage.
She turned the dial to the Shield’s channel.
Voices poured out of it, all at once.
“Third squad, we’re cut off!”
“Who’s in command? Anyone?”
“They’re over the canal!”
Nobody answered them.
Down the street a rifle stopped firing, and someone screamed.
The fighting was here. She left the dial where it was.
She took the nearest roof by its fire ladder.

A Shield officer crouched behind the parapet, shouting into the handset of the radio set on his back. Men in dark uniforms lay along the roof’s edge behind him. He had gray in his beard and a rank armband on his sleeve, and nobody on the channel was listening to him.
He looked at her coat, then at her face.
“You’re Lesley,” he said. “The rail yard.”
He held out the handset. She said her name into it, and for a moment the channel went quiet.
“All squads, to me! Hold the avenues!”
“Second, moving!”
“Fourth! On you!”
They held, barely.
Enders pushed at her district from three sides. Lesley lay on the parapet and fired. Each time a chest split open to strike, she put a round into it and worked the bolt for the next.
“Canal bridge! It’s on the bridge!”
“Mine,” said Lesley, and the one on the bridge went down.
The barrel grew hot. Where her left hand held it, it burned through her glove. She did not let go.
The base is behind me,
she thought.
Hold here, and nothing reaches it.
Between shots she looked out across the city.
Half of it was burning, the half with the base in it. Every swarm she could see was leaning on her district.
One thing was not.

Far off, in the middle of the city, a giant was walking, hundreds of meters tall. The firelight caught its black and gold. Nothing stood in its way. Every squad that might have stopped it was out here at the edge, with her.
It was walking toward the water. Toward the base.
Lesley was on her feet. “No! It’s a decoy!”

media.alt: Far off between the towers, a giant black and gold Ender walks through the burning city at night; then on a rooftop Lesley, in red and white, flings out an arm and shouts, an officer with a rank armband at her side and soldiers in dark uniforms below.

segs.t: The officer stared at her. “What?”
“They’re holding us here,” she said. “So that can walk in.”
She shoved the handset back into his hands. “Hold here!”
“Where are you going?”
She was already running.
No call of hers could reach the base from out here. She would have to bring the warning herself.
She ran over the rooftops toward the water. She jumped the gaps. Where a footbridge had fallen between two buildings, she climbed down its wreck and up the other side.
Ahead, by the water, a new siren started. She knew its note. Every week since her first day she had heard it tested.
The base’s alarm.
They know now,
she thought.
Fifty steps to the shelter. They know the way.
She had paced those steps herself, on her first morning there.
Over the base’s grounds, small craft the size of cars dipped and fired. Flames rose by the water, where the storehouse stood.

media.alt: Seen from the street at night, flying craft with bright lamps pass low over the towers while people below stare up at them.

segs.t: The roofs ran out at a wide street. She went down a drainpipe into the crowd.
Everyone was running away from the water. Lesley pushed the other way. Shoulders struck her. A man caught her arm.
“Wrong way! It’s down there!”
She pulled free, found a fire stair and went up it to the roofs again.
The giant had stopped. Its head was bent toward the base’s yard.
Its chest plates parted, and a light began to grow inside.
On her left side, the eye drew a thin teal ring around the glow. The ring was no bigger than a coin.
For years on the wall she had waited for that opening. It was open now, and out of range. No rifle she had ever fired could carry that far.
She knelt, rested the barrel on the ledge and fired anyway. She worked the bolt and fired again.
The rounds dropped somewhere into the burning streets between.
The giant fired first.
A white beam came down on the base’s yard. For a moment every roof on the shore stood out sharp.
The fifty steps,
she thought.
They cross that yard.
Then the light was gone. The giant straightened and walked away into the dark.
Lesley ran.
The base’s gate stood open, and she came through it.
The storehouse was burning. The lab still stood, its windows red with the alarm.
Fifty steps from the lab door to the shelter. Twenty steps short of the shelter, the ground was gone.
A crater lay there, smoking. At its edge a small figure knelt in the soot.
Across the crater, something tall and gray stepped up to the rim. It turned toward the child. Its arm came up, and its chest opened to strike.
Lesley fired.
The Ender toppled backward off the far rim.

media.alt: A small figure sits atop a heap of smoking rubble with fire behind it; then, as the smoke thins, Lesley stands in the ruins with her rifle while an Ender with a glowing chest falls through the air above her.

segs.t: Chang’e’s head came up. She looked at Lesley. Her glasses had slid down her nose. Behind them her eyes had filled, and the tears ran down through the soot.
“Chang’e,” said Lesley.
Lesley crossed the last of the yard and dropped to her knees in the ash. It was still hot.
Minutes,
she thought.
I was minutes away.
She pulled Chang’e against her coat and held on. The child’s lab coat was black with soot, and her hair smelled of smoke. Her small arms hung at her sides.
Over her head, Lesley looked for two white coats.
There was only the crater. Its floor was bare and black.
Nine days ago at the gate, Chang’e’s mother had held out her hand, and this time Lesley had taken it. Chang’e’s father had laid his on her shoulder, once.
They stood in front of her,
Lesley thought.
That was my place.
She held Chang’e tighter. “I’m... sorry.”
The small hands came up between them. One of them had held her sleeve for a promise. Now both pressed flat against her coat and pushed, as hard as they could.
Lesley let go.
Chang’e did not look at her. She barely moved her lips. “Leave me alone...”
Lesley’s hands stayed open in the air, stopped halfway, as they had in her first weeks at the base. Through the burned glove, her left palm showed raw.
Chang’e looked down at her own fingers.
Neither of them moved.
Why weren’t you there?
Lesley asked herself.
She had the answers. The order. Nine days with the comm switched off. Squads with nobody leading them. The swarms at the edge, and the giant walking in behind them.
Every one of them was true. Said here, to this child, each one would sound like an excuse.
Once she had sat in the rain between her own parents. She knew what this was better than anyone. She had let it happen to Chang’e.
Lesley stood. She brought her rifle up and turned to the Enders still coming down the street outside the gate. She did not look back.

media.alt: Chang'e and Lesley stand back to back in the firelight, both looking down and away from each other.

segs.t: She held that street until the Enders stopped coming. None of them came through the gate.
Then she climbed to a far roof up the shore, where she could see the base’s yard and the lab’s windows.
The yard was empty. The sky was still red from the fires. In the lab, one window was lit with the pale glow of the console.
Lesley sat down with the rifle across her knees and kept that window in her sights.
Leave me alone,
Chang’e had said, so low that Lesley had hardly heard it. In the dream, years later, it would be a shout.
Lesley would leave her alone. She would do it from here.
The giant had walked straight to the base. Lesley had carried the piece in through that gate, in her own fist.
Did they come for it?
She did not know.
Before dawn she turned the dial on her collar to the base’s channel. It hissed. Nobody called.
She left it there.
She did not lie down. When the sky went gray, the window was still lit, and Lesley was still watching it.
The next night she climbed the same roof. The window was lit again. She sat down and kept it in her sights.
